AI is rapidly rewriting the process and paperwork layer for Orthodontists, but on-site judgment and professional experience still rest with people. This article breaks down the specific impact and how to respond.

It does not suit people with unsteady hands, those who fear lengthy education, or those who cannot tolerate slow treatment. Orthodontic results take time and follow-ups are frequent, so carelessness can be dangerous.
A common path is: start with dental medicine → work as a dentist → complete orthodontic specialty training → treat patients independently → become an orthodontic director or open a clinic.
This work suits people with steady hands, attention to detail, patience, and aesthetic sensitivity. If you accept lengthy training and precision procedures, you can build a stable career here.

Orthodontists lead the diagnosis and treatment of dentofacial abnormalities, integrate imaging, models, and treatment plans, use clinical procedures and appliances, fit orthodontic devices, and track progress through follow-up visits.

paragraphs: In the morning, evaluate new patients and set treatment plans. During the day, bond brackets, adjust archwires, and fit clear aligners. Around midday, review follow-up progress. In the afternoon, manage complications. Before leaving, document treatment and schedule the next follow-up visit.

In short: straighten misaligned teeth. Tasks include collecting images, setting plans, fitting orthodontic appliances, following up, managing complications, and overseeing treatment courses. It combines manual and intellectual work on the front line of dental aesthetics.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 5,900 orthodontists were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to rise to 6,200 by 2034, a net increase of about 300 jobs, with about 200 openings annually and a 2024 median annual salary of ≥$239,200 (highest BLS OES bracket, 2026).

AI will not replace orthodontists, but it will take over treatment planning. Imaging and AI planning accelerate standard cases, shifting doctors from arranging teeth toward clinical procedures, complex cases, and patient communication. Pure standard planning will be displaced, while people with clinical expertise and operating skills will be more secure.
